# The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system*

[Original Article Link](/library/WK0P2S)

---

## Summary

The <u>cerebrum</u> (<u>telencephalon</u>) is the largest part of the <u>brain</u> and comprises the <u>cerebral cortex</u> and subcortical structures (e.g., <u>basal ganglia</u>, <u>hippocampus</u>). The longitudinal <u>fissure</u> divides the <u>brain</u> into two hemispheres. The cortex represents the top-outer layer of the <u>brain</u>, which receives its convoluted appearance from a network of <u>gyri</u> and sulci. Sulci separate the <u>cerebral cortex</u> further into a frontal, temporal, parietal, and <u>occipital lobe</u>. The <u>cerebrum</u> is the key structure involved in perception, language, and coordination. The <u>basal ganglia</u> are situated beneath the cortex, and they are heavily involved in motor control. The cortical hemispheres contain one of the <u>lateral ventricles</u> each, with the smaller third and <u>fourth ventricles</u> being located between the two thalami in the <u>diencephalon</u> and between the <u>cerebral aqueduct</u> and obex respectively. The four ventricles form an interconnected system that produces, drains, and is filled with <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u>, which plays a role in waste removal and cushioning of the <u>brain</u>. The <u>meninges</u> comprise the three protective membranes that envelop the <u>central nervous system</u>, i.e. the <u>brain</u> and spinal cord.

---

## Cerebral cortex

### Overview




* The <u>cerebral cortex</u> receives its convoluted appearance from a network of gyri (rounded ridges on the surface of the cortex) and sulci (furrows separating the <u>gyri</u>).

* The longitudinal <u>fissure</u> divides the <u>brain</u> into two hemispheres.

* Deep sulci divide each hemisphere further into a frontal, temporal, parietal, and <u>occipital lobe</u>.

* Deep sulci separate the <u>cerebral cortex</u> into different lobes: frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital

* The main sulci

* Central sulcus (of Rolando): separates the frontal and <u>parietal lobes</u>

* Lateral sulcus (Sylvian <u>fissure</u>): separates the frontal and <u>temporal lobes</u> anteriorly and the parietal and <u>temporal lobes</u> posteriorly

* Cingulate sulcus: separates the <u>cingulate gyrus</u> from the frontal and <u>parietal lobes</u>

* Parieto-occipital sulcus: separates the parietal and occipital lobes

* Calcarine sulcus: divides the <u>occipital lobe</u> horizontally into the cuneus (superior) and lingual (inferior) <u>gyrus</u>

### Frontal lobe




| Overview of the <u>frontal lobe</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Location | Motor and cognitive functions | Effect of lesion |
| <br>Primary motor cortex  (<u>Brodmann area 4</u>) | <br>* Precentral <u>gyrus</u> on the <u>frontal lobe</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Initiation of voluntary movement<br><br>* Gives rise to <u>axons</u> that form the <u>corticospinal tract</u><br><br>* The cortical regions responsible for processing the motor functions of the different regions of the body can be mapped using the motor homunculus.  <br><br>* The individual parts of the body are arranged against the corresponding cortical regions proportionate in size to their degree of innervation (e.g., the hand is represented disproportionately larger than the foot).<br><br>* Arranged medially to laterally as follows: toes, ankle, knee, hip, trunk, shoulder, <u>elbow</u>, wrist, hand, little finger to thumb, <u>eye</u>, facial expression, mouth, chin, <u>tongue</u>, <u>swallowing</u>.<br><br>* The primary sensory cortex is mapped in the same way using the <u>sensory homunculus</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>upper motor neuron</u> dysfunction (e.g., <u>contralateral</u> movement <u>paralysis</u>)<br><br>* Lesions in the paracentral lobule can cause <u>urinary incontinence</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Premotor cortex  (<u>Brodmann area 6</u>) | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> to the precentral <u>gyrus</u> on the <u>frontal lobe</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Contributes to the <u>corticospinal tract</u><br><br>* Involved in control of axial and <u>proximal</u> muscles<br><br>* Informs the <u>primary motor cortex</u> before execution of movements<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Apraxia</u><br><br> |
| <br>Frontal eye field (<u>Brodmann area 8</u>) | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> part of the middle frontal <u>gyrus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Controls voluntary <u>saccadic</u> <u>eye movements</u><br><br>* Stimulation causes <u>contralateral</u> conjugate deviation of the eyes<br><br><br> | <br>* Transient <u>ipsilateral</u> conjugate deviation of the eyes<br><br> |
| <br>Prefrontal cortex (<u>prefrontal association area</u>) | <br>* Connected to the <u>mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Higher cognitive functions (e.g., goal-setting, decision-making)<br><br>* Short term <u>memory</u><br><br>* Concentration<br><br>* Contains Brodmann areas 8–14, 24, 25, 32, and 45–47<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Frontal lobe</u> syndrome, <u>frontotemporal dementia</u><br><br>* <u>Personality</u> changes<br><br>* Aggressive behavior<br><br>* Social and sexual disinhibition<br><br>* <u>Tremor</u><br><br>* <u>Dystonia</u><br><br> |
| <br>Broca area  (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> part of the inferior frontal <u>gyrus</u> (dominant hemisphere)<br><br> | <br><br>* Area responsible for processing speech<br><br>* Connected to <u>Wernicke area</u> via the <u>arcuate fasciculus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Broca aphasia</u><br><br>* Nonfluent, telegraphic, and grammatically incorrect speech<br><br>* Intact comprehension of simple language<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The cortical regions responsible for processing the motor functions of the different regions of the body can be mapped using a <u>motor homunculus</u>.

### Parietal lobe




| Overview of the <u>parietal lobe</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Location | Characteristics (sensory functions) | Effect of lesion |
| <br>Primary somatosensory cortex <br> | <br>* <u>Postcentral gyrus</u> (<u>parietal lobes</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Receives input from the <u>ventral</u> <u>posterior</u> <u>nuclei</u> of the <u>thalamus</u><br><br>* Contributes to the <u>corticospinal tract</u><br><br>* The cortical regions receiving sensory input of the different regions of the body can be mapped using the sensory homunculus. <br><br>* The individual parts of the body are arranged against the corresponding cortical regions proportionate in size to their degree of innervation (e.g., the <u>lips</u> are represented disproportionately larger than the feet).<br><br>* The <u>primary motor cortex</u> is mapped in the same way using the <u>motor homunculus</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Contralateral</u> sensory loss<br><br> |
| Somatosensory association cortex | <br>* Superior parietal lobule and supramarginal <u>gyrus</u><br><br> | <br>* Integrates palpatory sensory information for pattern recognition<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>astereognosis</u> (loss of ability to identify an object by tactile input alone)<br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> astatognosis (loss of ability to recognize the position of one's own body parts)<br><br>* <u>Apraxia</u> (loss of ability to perform coordinated, purposeful, and/or learned movements when asked, even if the request is understood)<br>* Most common type: facial <u>apraxia</u> (loss of ability to coordinate and execute facial movements, like whistling or winking)<br><br>* <u>Conduction aphasia</u> (e.g., loss of ability to repeat verbal commands)<br>* Due to damage of the arcuate fasciculus (a <u>white matter</u> bundle connecting the frontal, parietal, and <u>temporal lobes</u> that plays a major role in language processing)<br><br><br> |
| Visual association cortex | <br>* Angular <u>gyrus</u><br><br> | <br>* Integrates visual sensory information for pattern recognition<br><br> | <br><br>* Injury to dominant hemisphere: Gerstmann syndrome<br><br>* Inability to recognize right or left<br><br>* Finger <u>agnosia</u> (loss of ability to distinguish or recognize one's own fingers or those of others)<br><br>* <u>Agraphia</u> (loss of ability to write down thoughts)<br><br>* Dyscalculia (loss of ability to do mathematical calculations)<br><br>* Unilateral injury to the nondominant hemisphere: <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemispatial neglect syndrome</u><br><br><br> |

### Temporal lobe




| Overview of the <u>temporal lobe</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Location | Characteristics (<u>hearing</u>) | Effect of lesion |
| <br>Primary auditory cortex  (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) | <br>* Transverse <u>gyrus</u> of the <u>temporal lobe</u><br><br> | <br>* Receives input from the <u>medial geniculate body</u><br><br> | <br><br>* One-sided <u>primary auditory cortex</u> lesions do not cause <u>hearing loss</u> because of bilateral representation of <u>hearing</u> on each side. I.e., a <u>primary auditory cortex</u> on the left receives auditory input from both sides, so does the right <u>primary auditory cortex</u>. Therefore, even if the <u>primary auditory cortex</u> on one side is damaged, the cortex on another side will be able to compensate for that.<br><br>* Bilateral <u>primary auditory cortex</u> lesions may lead to cortical deafness.<br><br>* Characterized by an inability to perceive both pure tones and complex sounds<br><br>* The <u>startle reflex</u> is preserved.<br><br>* Bilateral <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> pattern is confirmed with <u>audiogram</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Wernicke area <br> | <br>* <u>Posterior</u> part of the superior temporal gyrus (superior portion of the <u>temporal lobe</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Part of the auditory association cortex (Brodmann area 22)<br><br>* Connected to <u>Broca area</u> via the <u>arcuate fasciculus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Dominant hemisphere: <u>Wernicke aphasia</u><br><br>* Nondominant hemisphere: <u>aprosodia</u><br><br><br> |

### Occipital lobe




| Overview of the <u>occipital lobe</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area | Location | Characteristics (visual functions) | Effect of lesion |
| <br>Primary visual cortex <br> | <br>* In the region of the <u>calcarine sulcus</u> (cuneus and lingual <u>gyrus</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Receives input from the <u>lateral geniculate body</u> via <u>optic radiations</u> (also known as visual radiations, <u>geniculocalcarine tract</u>)<br><br>* Controls involuntary pursuit and tracking <u>eye movements</u><br><br>* Stimulation causes <u>contralateral</u> conjugate deviation of the eyes<br><br><br> | <br>* Difficulty tracking slow movements and/or <u>contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopsia</u><br><br> |
| <br>Secondary visual cortex <br> | <br><br>* <u>Occipital lobe</u><br><br>* Surrounds the <u>primary visual cortex</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Integrates visual properties such as color, position in space, and illusory contours<br><br> | <br>* <u>Visual hallucinations</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Bilateral or large unilateral (esp. right-sided) lesions in the <u>ventral</u> occipitotemporal cortex may cause impairment of facial recognition (<u>prosopagnosia</u>).

### Insular lobe




* Location

* Small region of the <u>cerebral cortex</u> deep within the Sylvian <u>fissure</u>

* Completely hidden below parts of the frontal, parietal, and <u>temporal lobes</u>

* Characteristics

* Receives input from the <u>thalamus</u> (sensory <u>thalamic nuclei</u>) and the <u>cerebral cortex</u>

* Reciprocally connected with the <u>limbic system</u> and frontal <u>brain</u> regions

* Function

* Processing of emotions

* Perception of body functions (<u>interoception</u>)

* Integration and perception of somatosensory stimuli

* Perception of gustatory and olfactory stimuli

* Modulation of autonomic functions (e.g., blood pressure, gastrointestinal motility)

### Internal capsule




* A deep subcortical structure that lies between the <u>basal ganglia</u>

* Largest collection of nerve fibers traveling to and from the <u>cerebral cortex</u>, forming the corona radiata (neuroanatomy), a collection of <u>white matter</u> fibers.

* Components: <u>anterior</u> limb, genu, and <u>posterior</u> limb  

* <u>Anterior</u> limb: contains the <u>thalamocortical tract</u>

* Genu: contains the <u>corticobulbar tract</u>

* <u>Posterior</u> limb: contains the <u>corticospinal tract</u> and thalamocortical and somatosensory fibers

## Meninges, falces, and spaces

### <u>Meninges</u>




* Three layers of <u>connective tissue</u> that cover and protect the <u>brain</u> and the spinal cord

* Divided into (from outer to inner layer): <u>dura mater</u>, <u>arachnoid mater</u>, and <u>pia mater</u>





| <br>Overview of the <u>meningeal layers</u> [[1]](/library/G_XBp00) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Meningeal layer</u> | Origin | Anatomy | Characteristics |
| Dura mater | <br>* <u>Mesoderm</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Outermost and thickest <u>meningeal layer</u><br><br>* Composed of dense, irregular <u>connective tissue</u><br><br>* Adheres to the <u>skull</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Forms the inner boundary of the <u>epidural space</u>: space between the <u>dura mater</u> and the bones of the <u>cranium</u>/<u>spine</u><br><br>* Forms the outer boundary of the <u>subdural space</u><br><br>* Folds to form septae: the <u>falx cerebri</u>, <u>falx cerebelli</u>, and <u>tentorium cerebelli</u> (See “<u>Falces of the brain</u>.”)<br><br><br> |
| Arachnoid mater | <br>* <u>Neural crest</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Middle layer between the <u>dura mater</u> and the <u>pia mater</u><br><br>* Composed of loose, translucent <u>connective tissue</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Forms the outer boundary of the <u>subarachnoid space</u><br><br> |
| Pia mater | <br><br>* Thin and fibrous inner layer<br><br>* Composed of fibrous <u>connective tissue</u> (e.g., <u>reticular fibers</u>, <u>collagen fibers</u>)<br><br>* Adheres to the <u>brain</u> and the spinal cord<br><br><br> | <br>* Forms the inner boundary of the <u>subarachnoid space</u><br><br> |  |

### Falces of the brain




| Overview of the <u>falces of the brain</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Location | Characteristics | Sites of attachment | <br><u>Cerebral sinuses</u><br> |
| <br>Falx cerebri <br> | <br>* Longitudinal <u>fissure</u><br><br> | <br>* Separates the cerebral hemispheres<br><br> | <br><br>* Crista galli of the <u>ethmoid bone</u> anteriorly<br><br>* Internal occipital protuberance posteriorly<br><br>* Midline of the <u>cranium</u> superiorly<br><br>* Superior surface of the <u>tentorium cerebelli</u> inferiorly<br><br><br> | <br><br>* The superior border contains the <u>superior sagittal sinus</u>.<br><br>* The inferior border contains the <u>inferior sagittal sinus</u>.<br><br>* The site of attachment to the <u>tentorium cerebelli</u> contains the straight sinus.<br><br><br> |
| Falx cerebelli | <br>* Floor of the <u>posterior cranial fossa</u><br><br> | <br>* Separates the two <u>cerebellar hemispheres</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tentorium cerebelli</u> superiorly<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> edge of the <u>foramen magnum</u> inferiorly<br><br>* Internal occipital crest posteriorly<br><br>* Edge that separates the <u>cerebellum</u> anteriorly<br><br><br> | <br>* Site of attachment to the internal occipital crest, which contains the occipital sinus<br><br> |
| Tentorium cerebelli | <br>* Perpendicular to the <u>falx cerebri</u> (in the <u>axial plane</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Separates the <u>cranial</u> cavity into infratentorial and supratentorial compartments<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Falx cerebri</u> on the midline<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> <u>clinoid processes</u> of the <u>sphenoid bone</u> anteriorly<br>* Forms the <u>lateral</u> part of the <u>cavernous sinus</u><br><br>* Petrous part of the <u>temporal bone</u> bilaterally (anterolateral margins)<br><br>* Posteroinferior angles of the parietal bone and transverse sulci of the <u>occipital bone</u> (posterolateral margins)<br><br>* Internal occipital protuberance posteriorly<br><br><br> | <br><br>* The midline attachment with the <u>falx cerebri</u> contains the straight sinus.<br><br>* The posterolateral attachments contain the <u>transverse sinus</u>.<br><br><br> |

### Spaces of the CNS




| Overview of the <u>spaces of the CNS</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Space | Description | Boundaries | Clinical significance |
| Epidural space | <br>* Spinal <u>epidural space</u>  <br><br>* Located within the <u>spinal canal</u> between the spinal <u>dura mater</u> and the <u>vertebral</u> wall<br><br>* Extends from the <u>base of the skull</u> to the <u>S2</u> <u>vertebra</u><br><br>* Contains <u>blood vessels</u>, <u>lymphatics</u>, and <u>fat tissue</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inner boundary: <u>dura mater</u><br><br>* Outer boundary: <u>posterior longitudinal ligament</u>, <u>intervertebral foramen</u>, <u>ligamentum flavum</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Application site for <u>epidural anesthesia</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Cranial</u> <u>epidural space</u>  <br><br>* Located between <u>dura mater</u> and <u>skull</u><br><br>* Potential space (<u>dura mater</u> adheres to the <u>skull</u>)<br><br>* Contains venous sinuses and the meningeal <u>arteries</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inner boundary: <u>dura mater</u><br><br>* Outer boundary: <u>skull</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Potential site of development for epidural pathologies (e.g., <u>epidural hematoma</u>, epidural <u>abscess</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Subdural space | <br>* Potential space between the <u>dura mater</u> and <u>arachnoid mater</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inner boundary: <u>arachnoid mater</u><br><br>* Outer boundary: <u>dura mater</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Potential site of development for subdural pathologies (e.g., <u>subdural hematoma</u>, subdural <u>empyema</u>, <u>subdural hygroma</u>)<br><br> |
| Subarachnoid space | <br><br>* The space between the <u>arachnoid layer</u> and <u>pia mater</u> that contains <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> (<u>CSF</u>).<br><br>* Extends from the <u>skull</u> to the <u>S2</u> <u>vertebra</u><br><br>* Contains major <u>arteries</u> of the <u>brain</u> (including the <u>circle of Willis</u>), the roots of the <u>spinal nerves</u>, and the <u>cauda equina</u><br><br>* Filled with <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* Site for <u>lumbar puncture</u> (diagnostic or therapeutic)<br><br>* Potential site for <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The Subarachnoid Space extends to the <u>S2</u> <u>vertebra</u>.

## Basal ganglia

### Overview




* The <u>basal ganglia</u> are a group of <u>nuclei</u> that lie beneath the cortex.

* Distributed over the <u>telencephalon</u>, <u>diencephalon</u>, and <u>mesencephalon</u> (<u>midbrain</u>)





| Overview of the <u>basal ganglia</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Basal ganglia</u> |  | Location | Clinical significance |
| Striatum | Caudate nucleus | <br>* <u>Telencephalon</u><br><br> | <br>* Molecular changes in <u>Huntington disease</u> lead to neuronal loss in the <u>striatum</u><br><br> |
| Putamen |  |  |  |
| Lentiform nucleus | Globus pallidus | <br>* <u>Diencephalon</u> .<br><br> | <br>* <u>Wilson disease</u> (<u>hepatolenticular degeneration</u>) leads to an impaired function of the <u>lentiform nucleus</u> due to <u>copper</u> accumulation.<br><br> |
| <u>Putamen</u> |  |  |  |
| Subthalamic nucleus |  | <br>* Effect of lesion: <u>contralateral</u> <u>hemiballismus</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Substantia nigra</u> |  | <br>* <u>Mesencephalon</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Parkinson disease</u> is characterized by neuronal degeneration in the <u>substantia nigra</u><br><br> |

### Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop (CBGTC)




* A neuronal circuit between the cortices of the <u>brain</u>, the <u>basal ganglia</u>, and the <u>thalamus</u>

* Via this loop, the <u>basal ganglia</u> aid in the initiation of movement, control of <u>skeletal muscles</u>, and adjustment of posture.

* Two main pathways: the direct pathway and the indirect pathway.

* The balance of activity between the direct and indirect pathways is modulated by <u>dopamine</u>.





![Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop (CBGTC)](media/y9g0mvp226qtps7w490otjh5.jpg)

Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop (CBGTC)




#### Functional anatomy of the <u>basal ganglia</u>




| <br>Overview of the functional anatomy of the <u>basal ganglia</u> <br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure |  | Function/Characteristics | <u>Neurotransmitter</u> | Motor activity |
| <u>Striatum</u> | Motor excitatory part | <br><br>* Inhibition of the Gpi<br><br>* Contains mainly D1 receptors, which are activated by <u>dopamine</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>GABA</u><br><br>* <u>Substance P</u><br><br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |
| Motor inhibitory part | <br><br>* Inhibition of the Gpe<br><br>* Contains mainly D2 receptors, which are inhibited by <u>dopamine</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>GABA</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> |  |
| Pallidum | Globus pallidus internus (Gpi) | <br>* Inhibition of the <u>thalamus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>GABA</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> |
| <br>Globus pallidus externus (Gpe) <br> | <br>* Inhibition of the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>GABA</u><br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |  |
| <u>Subthalamic nucleus</u> |  | <br><br>* Stimulation of the Gpi<br><br>* Stimulation of the pars reticularis of the <u>substantia nigra</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Glutamate</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> |
| <u>Substantia nigra</u> | Pars compacta | <br><br>* Stimulation of the motor excitatory part of the <u>striatum</u><br><br>* Inhibition of the motor inhibitory part of the <u>striatum</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Dopamine</u><br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |
| Pars reticularis | <br>* Inhibition of the <u>thalamus</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>GABA</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> |  |





![Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop (CBGTC)](media/y9g0mvp226qtps7w490otjh5.jpg)

Cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop (CBGTC)




#### Direct pathway of the basal ganglia (excitatory)




* Function: increase in motor activity

* Pathway

* Motor cortex activation → <u>glutamate</u> release → <u>striatum</u> stimulation → <u>GABA</u> release → inhibition of Gpi → inhibition of <u>GABA</u> release from the Gpi → <u>thalamus</u> disinhibition → <u>premotor cortex</u> stimulation → muscle activation → increased movement

* In addition, the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> stimulates the <u>substantia nigra</u> (pars compacta) → <u>dopamine</u> release → stimulation of <u>D1 receptors</u> in <u>striatum</u> → further inhibition of Gpi → inhibition of <u>GABA</u> release → <u>thalamus</u> disinhibition → <u>premotor cortex</u> stimulation → muscle activation → increased movement





> [!NOTE]
> The direct pathway facilitates movement.




> [!NOTE]
> Binding of <u>dopamine</u> to D1 Receptors stimulates the excitatory D1Rect pathway.




#### Indirect pathway of the basal ganglia (inhibitory)




* Function

* Decrease in motor activity

* Modulation of the disinhibitory effect of the direct pathway

* Pathway

* Motor cortex activation → <u>glutamate</u> release → stimulation of <u>striatum</u> (<u>medium spiny neurons</u>) → <u>GABA</u> release → inhibition of Gpe → decreased <u>GABA</u> release from Gpe → disinhibition (increased activity) of <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> → <u>glutamate</u> release → stimulation of <u>substantia nigra</u> (pars reticularis) and Gpi → <u>GABA</u> release from Gpi → inhibition of <u>thalamus</u> → reduced excitatory output to the motor cortex → deactivation of muscles → ↓ movement

* The <u>striatum</u> also stimulates the <u>substantia nigra</u> (pars compacta) → <u>dopamine</u> release → stimulation of <u>D2 receptor</u> in <u>striatum</u> → inhibition of <u>GABA</u> release → disinhibition of Gpe → <u>GABA</u> release → inhibition of <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> → ↓ stimulation of GPi → disinhibition of <u>thalamus</u> → ↑ movement





> [!NOTE]
> The indirect pathway inhibits movement.




> [!NOTE]
> Binding of <u>dopamine</u> to D2 Receptors results in double inhibition (i.e., inhibition of the inhibitory indirect pathway) resulting in increased movement.




### Dopaminergic pathways




* <u>Dopaminergic pathways</u> are collections of <u>neurons</u> that release <u>dopamine</u>.

* Dysfunction of <u>dopaminergic pathways</u> is involved in some psychiatric diseases (e.g., <u>schizophrenia</u>), addiction disorders, and movement disorders (e.g., <u>Parkinson disease</u>).

* <u>Antipsychotic drugs</u> target <u>dopaminergic pathways</u>.





| <br>Overview of <u>dopaminergic pathways</u> <br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pathway | Location | Characteristics | Defect |
| Nigrostriatal | <br>* From <u>substantia nigra</u> to <u>striatum</u> (<u>putamen</u> and <u>caudate nucleus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Controls <u>motor function</u><br><br> | <br>* Altered activity causes <u>extrapyramidal symptoms</u> and movement disorders (<u>parkinsonism</u> in the case of inhibition, <u>chorea</u> in the case of stimulation).<br><br> |
| Tuberoinfundibular | <br>* From the arcuate <u>nucleus</u> (infundibular <u>nucleus</u>) in the <u>hypothalamus</u> to the median eminence<br><br> | <br>* <u>Dopamine</u> release inhibits <u>prolactin</u> secretion from the <u>anterior pituitary</u>.<br><br> | <br><br>* Inhibition causes ↓ <u>dopamine</u> → ↑ <u>prolactin</u> → <u>galactorrhea</u>, <u>sexual dysfunction</u>, ↓ libido<br><br>* <u>Antipsychotic drugs</u> significantly affect this pathway.<br><br><br> |
| Mesolimbic | <br>* From the <u>ventral</u> tegmental area (VTA) to the nucleus accumbens and olfactory tubercle<br><br> | <br>* Controls the motivation and reward systems of the <u>brain</u> (e.g., pleasure, <u>positive reinforcement</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Stimulation causes positive symptoms (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>)<br><br>* Primary target for <u>antipsychotic drugs</u> used in the treatment of <u>schizophrenia</u> (e.g., <u>haloperidol</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Mesocortical | <br>* From the <u>ventral</u> tegmental area (VTA) to the <u>prefrontal cortex</u><br><br> | <br>* Controls <u>executive functions</u>, motivation, and reward systems of the <u>brain</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Inhibition causes <u>negative symptoms</u> (e.g., <u>apathy</u>, lack of energy).<br><br>* <u>Antipsychotic drugs</u> have limited <u>efficacy</u>.<br><br><br> |





![Dopaminergic pathways](media/oezrv671v49vvn0hnemqespn.jpg)

Dopaminergic pathways

## Ventricular system

### Overview




* Consists of four interconnected cavities within the <u>brain</u>: the two <u>lateral ventricles</u>; the <u>third ventricle</u>, located in the <u>diencephalon</u>; and the <u>fourth ventricle</u>, located <u>dorsal</u> to the <u>pons</u>

* Involved in the production and circulation of <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> (<u>CSF</u>)

* <u>CSF</u> serves as a fluid cushion and removes waste products from the <u>brain</u>





| <br>Overview of the <u>ventricular system</u> <br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ventricle | Anatomy | Drainage |
| Lateral ventricles | <br><br>* Paired (right and left)<br><br>* Located in the cerebral hemispheres<br><br><br> | <br>* Into the <u>3<sup>rd</sup> ventricle</u> via the paired interventricular foramina (of Monro)<br><br> |
| Third ventricle | <br><br>* Single midline ventricle<br><br>* Located in the <u>diencephalon</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Into the <u>4<sup>th</sup> ventricle</u> via the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)<br><br>* Passes through the <u>midbrain</u><br><br>* Located <u>dorsal</u> to the <u>pons</u> and <u>ventral</u> to the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br> |
| Fourth ventricle | <br><br>* Single midline ventricle<br><br>* Located <u>dorsal</u> to the <u>pons</u> and upper medulla<br><br><br> | <br>* Into the <u>subarachnoid space</u><br><br>* Laterally via the paired lateral apertures (<u>foramina of Luschka</u>)<br><br>* Medially via median aperture (<u>foramen of Magendie</u>)<br><br> |





![Ventricular system of the brain](media/zsvk5v9mdotvuq4spmtk05ub.jpg)

Ventricular system of the brain




> [!NOTE]
> The foramina of Luschka are the Lateral apertures and the foramen of Magendie is the Medial aperture of the <u>fourth ventricle</u>.




### Cerebrospinal fluid




* Description: a clear and colorless fluid derived from blood plasma that provides mechanical support to the <u>CNS</u> and transports biochemical compounds (e.g., neuromodulators) and waste products

* CSF production: produced by <u>choroid plexuses</u> in the <u>lateral</u>, third, and <u>fourth ventricles</u> by filtration of plasma

* CSF flow: <u>lateral ventricles</u> → <u>third ventricle</u> (via <u>interventricular foramina</u>) → <u>fourth ventricle</u> (via <u>cerebral aqueduct</u>) → <u>diffusion</u> and active transfer into the <u>subarachnoid space</u> (via <u>foramina of Luschka</u> and Magendie) → reabsorption in the arachnoid granulations (a group of projections of the <u>arachnoid mater</u> into the dural sinuses) → drainage into the <u>dural venous sinuses</u>





### Basal cisterns (<u>subarachnoid cisterns</u>)




* Description

* Numerous compartments within the <u>subarachnoid space</u> formed by a separation of the <u>pia mater</u> and arachnoid membrane, filled with <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u>

* Contain <u>arteries</u>, <u>veins</u>, and nerves

* Interconnected and essential for <u>CSF</u> circulation

* Cisterna magna

* Largest of the <u>basal cisterns</u>

* Located <u>posterior</u> to the medulla

* The <u>median aperture</u> and the <u>lateral apertures</u> drain <u>CSF</u> into the <u>cisterna magna</u>.

* Clinical relevance

* <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Mass effect</u> in accumulation of <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u>

* Arachnoid cyst: common, benign, and usually asymptomatic cystic lesion containing <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u>

## Microscopic anatomy

### Overview




* The nervous system is primarily composed of:

* <u>Neurons</u>: polarized cells with the ability of transmitting signals from one cell to another  

* Pyramidal cell: principal <u>neurons</u> of the <u>cerebral cortex</u> required for motor control and <u>cognition</u>

* Stellate cells (brain): star-shaped interneurons whose <u>axons</u> do not extend beyond the cortex

* Supporting <u>glial cells</u>

* For more information on the microscopic anatomy of the neurological tissue, see “<u>Nerve tissue</u>.”

* Cortical neuroanatomy

* The <u>cerebral cortex</u> can be divided into the <u>neocortex</u> and <u>allocortex</u>.

* Can also be divided into 47 Brodmann areas, defined by their cytoarchitecture.

* The <u>blood-brain barrier</u> separates the <u>brain</u> tissue from circulating blood and provides protection (e.g., from microorganisms, drugs)

* The <u>blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier</u> separates the <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> from the blood circulation.





![Types of neurons](media/xpvmx8m8hv4z8ghfn2l8ak5i.jpg)

Types of neurons

![Structure of a neuron](media/x6u05vc7zkv4umnzkmpfgrd1.jpg)

Structure of a neuron

### Cortical neuroanatomy




#### Neocortex




* Makes up the majority of the <u>cerebral cortex</u>

* Responsible for high-level processes (e.g., sensory perception, <u>cognition</u>, language skills)

* Layers:  

* <u>Molecular layer</u>: nerve fibers

* External granular layer

* Densely packed, small nonpyramidal cells (e.g., stellate cells)

* Small <u>pyramidal cells</u> that project <u>axons</u> to other cortical areas

* External pyramidal layer: small to medium-sized <u>pyramidal cells</u> that project <u>axons</u> to other cortical areas

* Internal granular layer

* Termination area of thalamocortical projections (form lines of Gennari in the <u>primary visual cortex</u>)

* Filled with densely packed, medium-sized pyramidal and nonpyramidal cells

* Internal pyramidal layer: large <u>pyramidal cells</u> give rise to the <u>axons</u> that form the <u>corticospinal tracts</u> and <u>corticobulbar tracts</u> (<u>pyramidal tracts</u> to the <u>brainstem</u> and spinal cord)

* Multiform layer: composed of pyramidal and nonpyramidal cells of various size





![Histological layers of the neocortex](media/b8w9m6w9ypbpo4sqxgbqas6j.jpg)

Histological layers of the neocortex




#### Allocortex




* Composed of three layers

* Consists of the <u>hippocampus</u> and the olfactory cortex





### Blood-brain barrier




* Description: a barrier of <u>CNS</u> <u>blood vessels</u> separating the <u>brain</u> from circulating blood

* Function: protects the <u>central nervous system</u> from microorganisms, cells, <u>proteins</u>, and drugs that can cause damage to the <u>brain</u> and other structures

* Components

* <u>Capillary</u> <u>endothelial</u> cells → have <u>tight junctions</u>

* The <u>basal lamina</u>

* <u>Astrocytes</u>

* Pericytes

* Transport mechanisms across the <u>blood-brain barrier</u>

* Ion channels (e.g., <u>sodium</u>, <u>potassium</u>)

* Selective transport (slow): <u>amino acids</u>, <u>glucose</u>, <u>vitamin K</u>, <u>vitamin D</u>

* <u>Diffusion</u> (fast): nonpolar and lipid-soluble substances (e.g., oxygen and carbon dioxide)

* Structures with no <u>blood-brain barrier</u>

* Structures located around the <u>brain</u> ventricles (circumventricular location), including:

* <u>Area postrema</u>: <u>vomiting</u> center (contains the <u>chemoreceptor trigger zone</u>)

* Organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (<u>OVLT</u>): <u>osmoreceptors</u>

* <u>Neurohypophysis</u>: <u>oxytocin</u> and <u>ADH</u> release directly into the blood

* Allow certain molecules to affect <u>brain</u> function (e.g., blood-borne drugs and <u>hormones</u>)

* Damage mechanisms

* <u>Brain</u> <u>infarction</u> and tumors break <u>endothelial</u> cell <u>tight junctions</u>, thereby causing <u>vasogenic edema</u>.

* Hyperosmolar solutions (e.g., <u>mannitol</u>) cause vasodilatation and shrinkage of <u>endothelial</u> cells, thereby disrupting the <u>blood-brain barrier</u> and increasing its permeability to other drugs.





![Blood-brain barrier](media/opj1bvmkw0d7l6evkfanypsj.jpg)

Blood-brain barrier




### Blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier (<u>BCSFB</u>)




* Function: separates <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> from the blood circulation

* Impermeable to cells, almost all <u>proteins</u>, and toxins (e.g., <u>hydrophilic</u> medications, bacteria)

* Selectively permeable to substances required for regulation and production of <u>CSF</u>, e.g., <u>glucose</u> and <u>electrolytes</u>

* Structure: formed by the choroid plexus

* Modified <u>ependymal cells</u> (<u>choroid</u> <u>epithelial</u> cells) held by <u>tight junctions</u>

* <u>Capillary</u> <u>endothelial</u> cells have fenestrations

* Basal membrane

* Choroid plexus carcinoma: a rare malignant <u>neoplasm</u> of the <u>choroid plexus</u> (∼ 1% of pediatric intracranial malignancies)

* Primarily occurs in children < 5 years

* Typically associated with signs of <u>hydrocephalus</u>, which can be caused by both increased <u>CSF production</u> and <u>CSF</u> outflow obstruction.

## Brain metabolism and homeostasis

### Brain metabolism [[2]](/library/3taSWm)[[3]](/library/w6chMW0)[[4]](/library/96cNMW0)




* Energy demand

* The <u>brain</u> requires 15% of the <u>cardiac output</u> and ∼ 20% of the body's oxygen to function properly. [[2]](/library/3taSWm)

* Main energy-demanding functions of the <u>brain</u>:

* Active transportation of ions

* Maintenance and restoration of membrane potentials

* Synthesis and metabolism of <u>neurotransmitters</u>

* Metabolic requirements vary according to regional neuronal activity and are directly related to changes in <u>cerebral blood flow</u> and energy substrate utilization (see “<u>Cerebral autoregulation</u>”).

* Energy sources

* Energy is mainly derived from the aerobic oxidation of <u>glucose</u>.

* The uptake of <u>glucose</u> by <u>neurons</u> is provided by the <u>insulin</u>-independent <u>GLUT3</u> transporter.

* Under particular circumstances, the <u>brain</u> has the capacity to use other energy substrates:

* <u>Ketone bodies</u> during prolonged <u>fasting</u>

* <u>Lactate</u> during periods of intense physical activity





### Brain homeostasis [[5]](/library/J6csNW0)




* Interactions between the <u>brain</u> and peripheral organs such as the <u>liver</u>, <u>pancreas</u>, <u>adipose tissue</u>, gut, and muscle are critical for the maintenance of energy and <u>glucose</u> <u>homeostasis</u>.

* The <u>blood-brain barrier</u> plays a key role by: [[6]](/library/N7c-Nd0)

* Exchanging substances between the blood and <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u>

* Modulating the response to extrinsic environmental factors and physiological changes (e.g., <u>sleep</u>/wake cycles, <u>aging</u>, diet) by adjusting its permeability

* The <u>choroid plexus</u> contributes by maintaining a constant <u>diffusion</u> of <u>nutrients</u> to the <u>CNS</u> through the <u>CSF</u>

* For more information, see “<u>Blood-brain barrier</u>” and “<u>Blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier</u>” in “The <u>cerebral cortex</u>, <u>meninges</u>, <u>basal ganglia</u>, and <u>ventricular system</u>.”

* The <u>hypothalamus</u> plays a key role in <u>homeostasis</u> by:

* Modulating energy intake and expenditure

* Modulating hepatic <u>glucose</u> production, <u>insulin</u> and <u>glucagon</u> secretion, and <u>skeletal muscle</u> <u>glucose</u> uptake, therefore maintaining <u>glucose</u> <u>homeostasis</u>

* Peripheral metabolic <u>hormones</u> and <u>nutrients</u> target <u>hypothalamic</u> neuronal circuits, providing feedback signals that help maintain this balance. (See “<u>Regulation of appetite</u> and satiety” in “<u>General endocrinology</u>”)

* <u>Cholecystokinin</u>, <u>peptide YY</u>, and <u>GLP-1</u> provide information on energy intake with meals.

* <u>Leptin</u> stimulates locomotor activity, <u>skeletal muscle</u> <u>fatty acid oxidation</u>, and <u>brown adipose tissue</u> <u>thermogenesis</u>, regulating <u>energy expenditure</u>.

* <u>Neuropeptide Y</u> and <u>POMC</u>-producing <u>neurons</u>, located in the <u>arcuate hypothalamic nucleus</u>, respond to neuroendocrine dysregulation.

* <u>Insulin</u> acts as an adipose signal, modulating <u>energy metabolism</u>.

* <u>IL-6</u> provides information on muscle mass and exercise and stimulates <u>energy expenditure</u> for active muscles.





> [!TIP]
> Impaired ability of the <u>brain</u> to maintain <u>homeostasis</u> may result in weight gain, <u>obesity</u>, and <u>diabetes mellitus type 2</u>.




![Hypothalamic-pituitary hormone axis](media/yvlmzw1srr1salysze8isrgl.jpg)

Hypothalamic-pituitary hormone axis

## Embryology of the brain

### Overview




* The <u>brain</u> is derived from 3 primary <u>vesicles</u>.

* <u>Prosencephalon</u> (forebrain)

* <u>Mesencephalon</u> (<u>midbrain</u>)

* <u>Rhombencephalon</u> (hindbrain)

* These <u>vesicles</u> develop into 5 subdivisions (<u>secondary brain vesicles</u>)

* <u>Prosencephalon</u> → <u>telencephalon</u> and <u>diencephalon</u>

* <u>Rhombencephalon</u> → <u>metencephalon</u> and <u>myelencephalon</u>

* <u>Mesencephalon</u>





### <u>Embryology of the brain</u>




| <br>Overview of <u>brain embryology</u> <br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary <u>vesicles</u> | <u>Brain</u> <u>vesicle</u> | Derived parts of the <u>brain</u> | Derived fluid-filled structure |
| <br>Prosencephalon (forebrain) | Telencephalon | <br><br>* Cerebral hemispheres<br><br>* Part of the <u>basal ganglia</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral ventricles</u><br><br> |
| Diencephalon | <br><br>* <u>Thalamus</u><br><br>* <u>Hypothalamus</u><br><br>* <u>Subthalamus</u><br><br>* <u>Pineal gland</u> (<u>epithalamus</u>)<br><br>* <u>Optic nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Retina</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Third ventricle</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Mesencephalon</u> (<u>midbrain</u>) | Mesencephalon | <br>* <u>Midbrain</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cerebral aqueduct</u><br><br> |
| <br>Rhombencephalon (hindbrain) | Metencephalon | <br><br>* <u>Cerebellum</u><br><br>* <u>Pons</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Fourth ventricle</u> (<u>rostral</u> portion)<br><br> |
| Myelencephalon | <br>* <u>Medulla oblongata</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Fourth ventricle</u> (<u>caudal</u> portion)<br><br> |  |





* Migration of <u>neurons</u> from the ventricular zone to the cortical zone during weeks 12–24 of <u>gestation</u> leads to the folding of the <u>cerebral cortex</u>. [[7]](/library/aOYQI6)[[8]](/library/fAYkQ7)

* Lissencephaly: failure of neuronal migration → lack of cortical sulci and <u>gyri</u> (<u>smooth brain</u>)

* Etiology: genetic mutations (e.g., of the reelin <u>gene</u>) or intrauterine viral infections during the <u>first trimester</u> of <u>pregnancy</u> (esp. <u>CMV</u>)

* Clinical features

* Typically manifests with <u>microcephaly</u>, <u>ventriculomegaly</u>, and craniofacial abnormalities

* Neurological deficits include <u>developmental delay</u>, <u>seizures</u>, and abnormalities of muscle tone (e.g., <u>dysphagia</u>, muscle spams).

* For more information on the <u>embryology</u> of the nervous system see “<u>Neurulation</u>” and “<u>Spinal cord tracts and reflexes</u>.”





> [!NOTE]
> Tell Di, Mes met My: The 1<sup>st</sup> <u>vesicle</u> is tel<u>encephalon</u>, 2<sup>nd</sup> is di<u>encephalon</u>, 3<sup>rd</sup> is mes<u>encephalon</u>, 4<sup>th</sup> is met<u>encephalon</u>, and 5<sup>th</sup> is myelencephalon (the order of the <u>secondary brain vesicles</u>).
